scenes.animation: Zippy spills dal curry on his white school shirt, leaving a yellow turmeric stain. He scrubs it with a soap bar and the stain turns reddish-brown; Zippy screams, and the soap bar screams too.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Help! The soap made the stain worse. It's turning red!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Relax. Rinse it with plenty of water and it'll turn yellow again. The turmeric in your curry is acting as an indicator.

scenes.animation: A kitchen shelf: lemon, curd, vinegar and imli under a banner 'ACIDS: sour'; a baking soda box and a soap bar under 'BASES: bitter, soapy to touch'. As Zippy reaches for a lab bottle, a red 'Never taste lab chemicals!' sign slams down.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Acids taste sour, like lemon juice, curd and vinegar. Bases taste bitter and feel soapy.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So I just lick things to check?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Never! We use indicators. They tell us whether a substance is acidic or basic by a change in colour or smell.

scenes.animation: A cartoon lichen on a rock squeezes purple dye into a bottle labelled 'Litmus (from lichen, Thallophyta)'. A blue litmus strip dips into dilute HCl and turns red; a red litmus strip dips into NaOH solution and turns blue.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Litmus is a purple dye extracted from lichen, a plant of the division Thallophyta. In a neutral solution, it stays purple.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Acids turn blue litmus red. Bases turn red litmus blue.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Other natural indicators include turmeric, red cabbage leaves, and coloured petals of hydrangea, petunia and geranium.

scenes.animation: Two test tubes: dilute HCl and NaOH solution. Drops of methyl orange make the acid red and the base yellow; drops of phenolphthalein leave the acid colourless and turn the base pink. A colour chart fills in beside them, row by row.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Synthetic indicators like methyl orange and phenolphthalein are used in the lab.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Methyl orange turns red in an acid and yellow in a base. Phenolphthalein stays colourless in an acid and turns pink in a base.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Pink means base. Got it.

scenes.animation: Chopped onions, a vanilla essence bottle and a clove oil vial stand on stage like singers, each with a smell cloud above. NaOH is added and the clouds vanish with a 'poof'; with HCl the clouds stay. A yellow 'BOARD TIP' card slides in with the indicator table.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Can an indicator work for someone who can't see colours?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes. Olfactory indicators change their odour. Onion, vanilla essence and clove oil lose their smell in a basic solution, but keep it in an acid.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: learn the full indicator table, litmus, methyl orange, phenolphthalein, turmeric and the olfactory ones. One-mark questions come straight from it.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three ticks: '1. Acids: sour, blue litmus → red. Bases: bitter, soapy, red litmus → blue', '2. Methyl orange: red/yellow. Phenolphthalein: colourless/pink', '3. Olfactory: onion, vanilla, clove lose smell in base'. Zippy's shirt, now clean, waves on a clothesline.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: acids are sour and turn blue litmus red; bases are bitter, soapy and turn red litmus blue.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base; phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: onion, vanilla and clove oil are olfactory indicators that lose their smell in a base.

name: Reaction of Acids and Bases with Metals

scenes.animation: Zippy blows soap bubbles from a tube connected to a bubbling test tube; one bubble drifts near a burning candle and goes 'POP!' with a tiny flash. Zippy's eyes spin like pinwheels.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: My bubble exploded! Did I just invent a new Diwali cracker?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No, you just did the test for hydrogen. That gas came from zinc reacting with an acid.

scenes.animation: The apparatus builds step by step with labels: a test tube with 'Zinc granules', 'Dilute H2SO4' poured in, a delivery tube leading into 'Soap solution', and 'H2 bubbles' forming. A burning candle approaches a bubble: 'POP'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Put zinc granules in a test tube and add dilute sulphuric acid. Bubbles of gas form on the surface of the zinc.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Pass the gas through soap solution to trap it in bubbles. Bring a burning candle near a bubble and it burns with a pop sound. That pop confirms hydrogen.

scenes.animation: 'Zn(s) + H2SO4(aq) → ZnSO4(aq) + H2(g)' assembles, then the general rule 'Acid + Metal → Salt + Hydrogen gas' appears in a gold frame. A swap card shows 'Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2'; the salt part flashes while H2 stays fixed.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Zinc and sulphuric acid give zinc sulphate and hydrogen. In general, acid plus metal gives salt plus hydrogen gas.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Does it work with hydrochloric acid too?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes. Zinc with hydrochloric acid gives zinc chloride and hydrogen. The salt changes with the acid, but the gas is still hydrogen.

scenes.animation: A test tube of sodium hydroxide solution with zinc granules is warmed; bubbles rise and a bubble pops at the candle again. Equation: '2NaOH(aq) + Zn(s) → Na2ZnO2(s) + H2(g)' with 'Sodium zincate' tagged under Na2ZnO2.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Okay, but bases can't do this. They're too soapy and calm.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Surprise. Warm zinc with sodium hydroxide solution, and hydrogen bubbles out again. This time the salt formed is sodium zincate.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: But careful: such reactions are not possible with all metals.

scenes.animation: A yellow 'BOARD TIP' card: 'Gas burns with a pop → H2'. Zippy practises writing 'Na2ZnO2' three times in a notebook; the third attempt gets a gold star.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: whenever a question says a gas burns with a pop sound, the answer is hydrogen.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: And write sodium zincate correctly: N a two Z n O two. Students often get this formula wrong.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: N a two Z n O two. Got my gold star!

scenes.animation: Recap board with three ticks: '1. Acid + Metal → Salt + H2', '2. H2 test: burning candle → pop sound', '3. 2NaOH + Zn → Na2ZnO2 + H2'. A last soap bubble floats up and pops into confetti.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: acid plus metal gives salt plus hydrogen gas, like zinc with dilute sulphuric acid.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: hydrogen burns with a pop sound when a burning candle is brought near it.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: some metals, like zinc, also react with sodium hydroxide to give hydrogen and a salt, sodium zincate.

name: Metal Carbonates, Metal Oxides and Neutralisation

scenes.animation: Zippy squeezes lemon over a pakora and a few drops land on the marble kitchen counter. The spot fizzes with tiny bubbles and the marble slab grows a frowning face.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: The counter is fizzing at me!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Marble is calcium carbonate, and lemon juice is acidic. Acids and carbonates always fizz together, Zippy.

scenes.animation: Lab: dilute HCl is added to sodium carbonate in a test tube; the gas passes through a delivery tube into lime water, which turns milky. Labels: 'Na2CO3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O + CO2' and 'Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O (milky)'. A second card: 'NaHCO3 + HCl → NaCl + H2O + CO2'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Add dilute hydrochloric acid to sodium carbonate and it fizzes. Pass the gas through lime water and the lime water turns milky. That's carbon dioxide.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Sodium hydrogencarbonate does the same. Metal carbonate or hydrogencarbonate plus acid gives salt, carbon dioxide and water.

scenes.animation: More CO2 keeps bubbling into the milky lime water until it turns clear again; label 'Excess CO2: CaCO3 + H2O + CO2 → Ca(HCO3)2 (soluble)'. Side icons of limestone, chalk and marble all wear the same 'CaCO3' badge.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I kept bubbling, and the milkiness disappeared!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Excess carbon dioxide forms calcium hydrogencarbonate, which is soluble in water. By the way, limestone, chalk and marble are all forms of calcium carbonate.

scenes.animation: A test tube of NaOH solution with two drops of phenolphthalein glows pink. Dilute HCl is added drop by drop until the pink suddenly vanishes; one drop of NaOH brings the pink back. Equation: 'NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)' with 'Base + Acid → Salt + Water' beneath.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now take sodium hydroxide solution with phenolphthalein. It's pink. Add dilute hydrochloric acid drop by drop.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: It went colourless!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The acid has cancelled the effect of the base. Add a drop of base and the pink returns. Base plus acid gives salt plus water. This is a neutralisation reaction.

scenes.animation: Black copper oxide powder in a beaker; dilute HCl is stirred in and the solution turns blue-green. Equation: 'CuO + 2HCl → CuCl2 + H2O' with a tag 'Metal oxide = basic'. A second card, 'Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O', is tagged 'Non-metal oxide = acidic'. A yellow 'BOARD TIP' note appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Copper oxide dissolves in hydrochloric acid to give blue-green copper chloride and water. It reacts like a base, so metal oxides are called basic oxides.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Carbon dioxide reacts with a base, calcium hydroxide, to give salt and water. So non-metal oxides are acidic.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: the lime water test, and why it clears with excess carbon dioxide, is a classic. Write both equations.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three ticks: '1. Carbonate/hydrogencarbonate + acid → salt + CO2 + H2O', '2. Base + Acid → Salt + Water (neutralisation)', '3. Metal oxides basic, non-metal oxides acidic'. The marble counter smiles again.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: carbonates and hydrogencarbonates react with acids to give salt, water and carbon dioxide, which turns lime water milky.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: acid plus base gives salt plus water; that's neutralisation.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: metal oxides are basic, and non-metal oxides are acidic.

name: What Acids and Bases Have in Common

scenes.animation: Zippy stands on a giant glucose molecule, counting its hydrogen atoms on his fingers. A banner 'C6H12O6: 12 hydrogens!' waves behind him and he crowns himself 'Acid King'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Glucose has twelve hydrogen atoms. That makes it the strongest acid ever!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Nice try, Your Majesty. Having hydrogen isn't enough. Let's test it with a bulb.

scenes.animation: Setup builds step by step: two nails fixed in a rubber cork inside a beaker, wired through a bulb and switch to a 6 V battery. The beaker is filled in turn with glucose solution (bulb dark), alcohol solution (dark), then dilute HCl (bulb glows). Tiny 'H+' ions zip between the nails.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In glucose or alcohol solution, the bulb stays off. In dilute hydrochloric acid, it glows.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Acids produce hydrogen ions in solution, and these ions carry the current. Glucose and alcohol contain hydrogen but don't release hydrogen ions, so they aren't acids.

scenes.animation: Dry HCl gas passes over a strip of dry blue litmus: nothing happens. A water droplet lands on the strip and it turns red. An 'H+' ion hops onto a water molecule to become 'H3O+'. Equation: 'HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl−'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So hydrogen chloride gas is always acidic?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Only with water. Dry HCl gas doesn't change the colour of dry litmus paper. Moist litmus turns red, because hydrogen ions form only in water.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Hydrogen ions can't exist alone. They combine with water molecules to form hydronium ions.

scenes.animation: Three base bottles release ions: 'NaOH → Na+ + OH−', 'KOH → K+ + OH−', 'Mg(OH)2 → Mg2+ + 2OH−'. A Venn diagram draws: a big circle 'Bases' with a smaller circle inside, 'Alkalis (soluble in water)'. Then 'H+ + OH− → H2O' shows two ions hugging into a water drop.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Bases produce hydroxide ions in water. Bases that are soluble in water are called alkalis.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So all alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis. And in neutralisation, hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions combine to form water.

scenes.animation: Split screen. Left, green tick: acid is poured slowly into a large beaker of water while a glass rod stirs. Right, red cross: water is poured into concentrated acid, which splashes and the beaker cracks. A thermometer mascot sweats between them. A yellow 'BOARD TIP' banner reads 'Acid to water, never water to acid'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Diluting is easy. Just pour water into the acid, right?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Dangerous! Mixing a concentrated acid with water is highly exothermic. Always add the acid slowly to water, with constant stirring.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Adding water to concentrated acid can make the mixture splash out and cause burns, and the glass container may break.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Dilution also lowers the concentration of hydronium or hydroxide ions per unit volume. Board tip: why acid must be added to water is a frequent reasoning question.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three ticks: '1. Acids give H+ (as H3O+) only in water; bases give OH−', '2. Alkalis = water-soluble bases', '3. Add acid to water slowly, with stirring'. Zippy hands his crown to a hydronium ion.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: acids produce hydrogen ions, as hydronium ions, only in water; bases produce hydroxide ions.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: bases that dissolve in water are alkalis. All alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: always add acid to water slowly while stirring, because the process is highly exothermic.

name: The pH Scale and pH in Everyday Life

scenes.animation: A school picnic. A bee stings Zippy and he zooms around in frantic circles, leaving a zigzag trail. Neo calmly opens a box of baking soda.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Owww! A bee stung me! Am I going to explode?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: You're fine. A bee sting leaves methanoic acid, which causes the pain. Rubbing a mild base like baking soda on it helps.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Wait, how acidic is acidic? Is there a score?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: There is. It's called pH.

scenes.animation: A long rainbow ruler slides across the screen, numbered 0 to 14: red at 0 labelled 'Very acidic', green at 7 'Neutral', violet at 14 'Very basic'. Drops of universal indicator land on lemon juice, water and soap solution and their colours match low, 7 and high positions on the ruler.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The pH scale runs from zero to fourteen. The p stands for 'potenz', German for power.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Seven is neutral. Below seven is acidic; above seven is basic. A universal indicator shows different colours along this scale.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So a lower number means more acidic?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes. The higher the hydrogen ion concentration, the lower the pH.

scenes.animation: Two acid bottles on a stage: a muscular 'Strong acid (HCl)' flinging handfuls of H+ ions, and a sleepy 'Weak acid (CH3COOH)' releasing only a few. The pH needle swings lower for the strong one.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Acids that give more hydrogen ions are strong acids. Acids that give fewer, like acetic acid, are weak acids.

scenes.animation: Montage: a human body silhouette with a gauge reading '7.0 – 7.8'; a rain cloud dripping 'pH < 5.6' into a river where cartoon fish look worried; a farmer testing soil with pH paper beside wheat plants.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Our body works within a narrow pH range of 7.0 to 7.8.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Rain with a pH less than 5.6 is acid rain. When it flows into rivers, it lowers their pH, and aquatic life finds it hard to survive.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Plants also grow best in soil of a particular pH.

scenes.animation: Inside a cartoon stomach, waves of excess acid crash around; a bottle labelled 'Milk of magnesia – Mg(OH)2' surfs in and calms them. Then a giant tooth with a shiny enamel shield; sugar-munching bacteria spit acid and a gauge drops below 5.5 as the shield cracks; toothpaste foam rushes in and the gauge rises. A yellow 'BOARD TIP' card flips.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Your stomach makes hydrochloric acid to help digestion. Too much causes pain and irritation, so we take antacids like milk of magnesia, a mild base.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Tooth enamel, calcium hydroxyapatite, is the hardest substance in the body. But tooth decay starts when the pH in the mouth falls below 5.5.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Bacteria make acids from leftover sugar and food. Toothpastes are basic, so they neutralise the excess acid.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: remember 5.5 for tooth decay and 5.6 for acid rain. Students often swap them.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three ticks: '1. pH 0–14: 7 neutral, < 7 acidic, > 7 basic', '2. More H+ → lower pH; strong vs weak acids', '3. pH in life: body 7.0–7.8, antacids, toothpaste, acid rain, bee sting'. Zippy wears a small plaster, smiling.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the pH scale goes from zero to fourteen; seven is neutral, below is acidic and above is basic.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: strong acids give more hydrogen ions, so they have a lower pH.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: pH matters in daily life, from antacids and toothpaste to acid rain and bee stings.

scenes.animation: A cartoon courtroom. Zippy, in a judge's wig, bangs a gavel: 'All salts are neutral!' A jury of salt crystals whispers; a washing soda crystal raises its hand and turns a strip of pH paper blue. Neo stands up as the lawyer.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Salts are made by neutralisation, so every salt must be neutral. Pure logic!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Objection, Your Honour. Let's test that with pH paper.

scenes.animation: A family tree: the 'Sodium family' branch holds NaCl, Na2SO4 and Na2CO3; the 'Chloride family' branch holds NaCl, KCl and NH4Cl. NaCl sits where the two branches cross, waving to both sides.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: First, salts come in families. Salts with the same positive or negative radical belong to the same family.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Sodium chloride and sodium sulphate are in the sodium family. Sodium chloride and potassium chloride are in the chloride family.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So sodium chloride has two families. Double the Diwali gifts!

scenes.animation: A row of test tubes labelled NaCl, KNO3, NH4Cl, Na2CO3, NaHCO3 and CH3COONa. Neo dips pH paper in each; readings flash: green '7', green '7', orange '< 7', blue '> 7', blue '> 7', blue '> 7'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Sodium chloride and potassium nitrate show pH seven. Ammonium chloride is below seven. Sodium carbonate, sodium hydrogencarbonate and sodium acetate are above seven.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So salts can be acidic, neutral or basic. Objection sustained.

scenes.animation: Tug-of-war cartoons: 'HCl (strong acid) vs NaOH (strong base)' stays centred on 'pH 7 – NaCl'; 'HCl (strong acid) vs NH4OH (weak base)' slides toward 'Acidic – NH4Cl'; 'H2CO3 (weak acid) vs NaOH (strong base)' slides toward 'Basic – Na2CO3'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It depends on the parents. Every salt comes from an acid and a base.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Sodium chloride comes from hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, both strong. So it's neutral.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ammonium chloride comes from a strong acid and a weak base, ammonium hydroxide, so it's acidic. Sodium carbonate comes from a weak acid, carbonic acid, and a strong base, so it's basic.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: The stronger parent wins the tug-of-war!

scenes.animation: A yellow 'BOARD TIP' table fades in, row by row: 'Strong acid + Strong base → pH 7', 'Strong acid + Weak base → pH < 7', 'Weak acid + Strong base → pH > 7'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: when asked for the pH of a salt, first write its parent acid and base. Then decide which one is strong. That one step answers most questions.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three ticks: '1. Salt families share a positive or negative radical', '2. Strong acid + strong base → neutral (pH 7)', '3. Strong acid + weak base → acidic; weak acid + strong base → basic'. Zippy hangs up his judge's wig.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: salts with the same positive or negative radical belong to one family.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: salts of a strong acid and a strong base are neutral, with pH seven.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: a strong acid with a weak base gives an acidic salt; a weak acid with a strong base gives a basic salt.

scenes.animation: Zippy flicks a single salt crystal off a pakora. The crystal swells into a tiny factory whose doors open, and out march NaOH, Cl2, bleaching powder, baking soda and washing soda like a band in a parade.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: It's just table salt. What's so special?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That crystal is the raw material for sodium hydroxide, chlorine, bleaching powder, baking soda and washing soda.

scenes.animation: An electrolysis tank of brine builds step by step: anode on the left bubbling greenish 'Cl2', cathode on the right bubbling 'H2', and 'NaOH solution' forming near the cathode. Equation: '2NaCl(aq) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + Cl2(g) + H2(g)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Pass electricity through brine, an aqueous solution of sodium chloride. It decomposes to form sodium hydroxide.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Chlorine gas is given off at the anode and hydrogen gas at the cathode. Sodium hydroxide forms near the cathode.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why is it called the chlor-alkali process?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Chlor for chlorine, alkali for sodium hydroxide. Sodium hydroxide is used for soaps and paper; chlorine for water treatment and PVC.

scenes.animation: Chlorine gas swirls over a tray of dry slaked lime and a white powder forms: 'Ca(OH)2 + Cl2 → CaOCl2 + H2O'. Use icons pop up: a cotton sari getting whiter, a paper mill, a water tank with a 'disinfected' tick.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Chlorine acting on dry slaked lime gives bleaching powder.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It bleaches cotton and linen, wood pulp, and washed clothes. It's an oxidising agent in industry, and it makes drinking water free of germs.

scenes.animation: A mixing card: 'NaCl + H2O + CO2 + NH3 → NH4Cl + NaHCO3'. Then a heating card: '2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2'. A cake in an oven rises as CO2 bubbles puff inside; label 'Baking powder = baking soda + tartaric acid'. Small icons: an antacid tablet and a soda-acid fire extinguisher.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Baking soda, sodium hydrogencarbonate, is made using sodium chloride, water, carbon dioxide and ammonia. It's a mild, non-corrosive base.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: On heating, it gives sodium carbonate, water and carbon dioxide. Mixed with a mild edible acid like tartaric acid, it becomes baking powder. The carbon dioxide released makes cakes soft and spongy.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It's also used in antacids and in soda-acid fire extinguishers.

scenes.animation: Sodium carbonate from heated baking soda dissolves and recrystallises into large clear crystals labelled 'Na2CO3·10H2O (washing soda)'. Use icons: a glass bottle, a soap bar, a paper roll, a borax jar, and a hard-water tap with a tick. A yellow 'BOARD TIP' card flips.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recrystallise sodium carbonate and you get washing soda, with ten water molecules in its formula.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It's used in the glass, soap and paper industries, to make borax, as a household cleaner, and to remove permanent hardness of water.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: for bleaching powder, baking soda and washing soda, learn one equation and two uses each.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three ticks: '1. Chlor-alkali: brine → NaOH + Cl2 + H2', '2. Cl2 + dry slaked lime → bleaching powder', '3. Baking soda (NaHCO3) and washing soda (Na2CO3·10H2O)'. The parade band from scene 1 takes a bow.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the chlor-alkali process, electrolysis of brine, gives sodium hydroxide, chlorine and hydrogen.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: chlorine with dry slaked lime gives bleaching powder, a bleach and disinfectant.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: baking soda makes cakes rise and fights acidity, while washing soda cleans and removes permanent hardness of water.

name: Water of Crystallisation and Plaster of Paris

scenes.animation: Zippy floats into the lab with a white plaster cast on one tiny arm, covered in cricket-team autographs. Neo taps the cast and it goes 'tok tok'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I dived for a catch and hurt my arm! The doctor wrapped it in this rock-hard stuff.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's Plaster of Paris. To understand it, we first need to find the water hidden inside crystals.

scenes.animation: Blue copper sulphate crystals are heated in a dry boiling tube; water droplets form on the upper walls and the crystals fade to white. A dropper adds two or three drops of water and the white powder flushes back to blue with a sparkle.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Heat blue copper sulphate crystals in a dry boiling tube. Water droplets appear, and the crystals turn white.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Where did the water come from? The crystals looked totally dry!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The water was part of the crystal. Add a few drops of water back, and the blue colour returns.

scenes.animation: Zoom into a crystal: each 'CuSO4' unit holds hands with five tiny water molecules. Labels pop in: 'CuSO4·5H2O', 'Na2CO3·10H2O', 'CaSO4·2H2O (gypsum)'. Heading: 'Water of crystallisation = fixed number of water molecules in one formula unit of a salt'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: This is water of crystallisation: the fixed number of water molecules present in one formula unit of a salt.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Copper sulphate has five, washing soda has ten, and gypsum, which is calcium sulphate, has two.

scenes.animation: Gypsum heats in a pan with a thermometer reading '373 K'. Equation: 'CaSO4·2H2O → CaSO4·½H2O + 1½H2O' with 'Heat, 373 K' above the arrow. Two CaSO4 units share one water molecule between them, like two friends sharing one cutting chai.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Heat gypsum at 373 kelvin. It loses water and becomes calcium sulphate hemihydrate. That's Plaster of Paris, a white powder.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Half a water molecule? Did someone cut it with a knife?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No. Two formula units of calcium sulphate share one water molecule, so we write half a water molecule per unit.

scenes.animation: Plaster of Paris powder is mixed with water into a paste that hardens into a solid block; equation 'CaSO4·½H2O + 1½H2O → CaSO4·2H2O'. Use icons: a bone cast, a toy figurine, a ceiling decoration, a smooth wall. A yellow 'BOARD TIP' card shows an airtight, moisture-proof tin.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Mix Plaster of Paris with water and it changes back into gypsum, a hard solid mass. That's your cast.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Doctors use it to support fractured bones in the right position. It's also used for toys, decorative materials, and making surfaces smooth.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: Plaster of Paris must be stored in a moisture-proof container, because moisture turns it into hard gypsum. This is a common question.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three ticks: '1. Water of crystallisation: CuSO4·5H2O, Na2CO3·10H2O, CaSO4·2H2O', '2. Gypsum → (373 K) → Plaster of Paris, CaSO4·½H2O', '3. PoP + water → gypsum (casts, toys, decoration)'. Zippy's cast now has Neo's autograph too.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules in one formula unit of a salt, like five in copper sulphate.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: heating gypsum at 373 kelvin gives Plaster of Paris, calcium sulphate hemihydrate.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: with water, it sets back into hard gypsum, used for casts, toys and decoration.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: And for collecting autographs!
